title: DOL Independent Contractor Rule Finalized: Score Every 1099 Sub on the Two Core Factors From the Books, Price the Cost to Convert by Job, and Fix the WIP Before January 22

mainEntity.name: Does the DOL independent contractor rule change how the IRS classifies my subs?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The rule applies only to the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act. The IRS keeps its common law test of behavioral control, financial control, and relationship, and states keep their own tests. A sub can be a contractor under the DOL rule and an employee under a state ABC test, and you must follow the stricter result.

mainEntity.name: When does the final rule take effect?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Department of Labor announced the final rule on November 19, 2026. It is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on November 23, 2026 and takes effect 60 days later, on January 22, 2027. The DOL says no affirmative action is required, but the effective date is the natural deadline for finishing the register and signing the conversion decisions.

mainEntity.name: What are the two core factors in the new test?

acceptedAnswer.text: The nature and degree of control over the work, and the worker's opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative or management of investment. When both point the same way, the DOL says that will almost always be the correct classification. Skill, permanence, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production matter mainly when the two core factors conflict.

mainEntity.name: How much more does a converted sub cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on whether you reset the wage or carry the 1099 rate. In the worked example, resetting a $55 per hour sub to a $44 wage plus burden and overtime costs about $54 per hour, close to the current cost. Carrying $55 as the wage costs about $68 per hour, 23 percent more. Workers compensation and the overtime premium drive most of the difference.

mainEntity.name: Should I book a reserve for past misclassification?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only when a loss is probable and can be reasonably estimated under ASC 450. Estimate the unpaid overtime premium over the two year lookback, three years if willful, plus an equal amount of liquidated damages, and record it as a period expense and an accrued liability rather than a job cost. If the loss is reasonably possible but not probable, disclose it instead of accruing it.

content:
The DOL independent contractor rule finalized on November 19, 2026 returns to a two-factor test: control over the work and opportunity for profit or loss. It takes effect January 22, 2027. A contractor should build the 1099 sub register from the books, score each sub, price the cost to convert by job, and update the WIP schedule first.

Most of the coverage so far is written for HR and employment counsel. It explains the factors and tells you to review your contractor roster. It doesn't tell a general contractor with 14 open jobs and 23 1099 vendors what the review costs, which jobs absorb it, or what happens to percent complete when a framing crew lead becomes a W-2 employee in February. That is the part a controller owns, and it is the part this article covers.

Why now: the rule is final, and January 22, 2027 is the date

The Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division announced the final rule on 2026-11-19. It rescinds the 2024 regulation and replaces it with a modified version of the 2021 analysis, applied uniformly under the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act. The DOL's FAQs published 2026-11-19 describe five non-exhaustive factors and name two of them core: the nature and degree of control over the work, and the worker's opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative or management of investment. Where both core factors point the same way, the DOL says that will almost always be the correct classification.

The rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on 2026-11-23 as document 2026-23777, and it takes effect 60 days later, on January 22, 2027. The DOL announcement said the February 2026 proposal drew roughly 16,500 comments. In practice the DOL's investigators have not applied the 2024 rule since Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-1 of 2025-05-01 told them to use the 2008 Fact Sheet #13 framework instead. So January is less a cliff than the point at which the core-factor test becomes the published standard that counsel, insurers, and auditors will cite.

Construction trade groups welcomed it. Associated Builders and Contractors called it a workable change the same day, and the National Association of Home Builders said it provides greater predictability for businesses that use independent contractors. The analyses from Littler, SHRM, and HRMorning list review and payroll steps. None of them price the conversion, allocate it to jobs, or say what the WIP schedule should show afterward. Those are the three questions below.

Build the 1099 sub register from the books and score the two core factors

Start with the ledger, not the contracts. The rule itself says actual practice outweighs contractual theory, and the ledger records practice. Pull every vendor flagged for a 1099-NEC in 2026 and, for each one, the fields below. If you ran the vendor payment test described in the 1099-NEC threshold article, you already have the first half.

  • Total paid in the year, number of payments, and cadence. Fifty-two payments of nearly the same amount look like payroll. Twelve progress payments against phase milestones look like a subcontract.
  • Jobs and accounts charged. A sub coded only to subcontractor expense on three jobs reads differently from one whose payments also hit tool reimbursements, fuel, and per diem.
  • What the invoices contain. Lump sum or unit price per phase, with the sub's own materials and equipment on the invoice, supports investment and profit or loss. Hours times a rate with nothing else supports neither.
  • Who buys the inputs. Equipment rentals, tool purchases, and materials you coded to that sub's scope are evidence that you carry the investment, not the sub.
  • Insurance and licensing on file. A current certificate of insurance for general liability and workers compensation, and a trade license in the sub's name, are investment and control evidence. The DOL's revised Fact Sheet #13 says that requiring a worker to carry insurance, meet safety standards, or hit agreed deadlines and quality standards does not by itself indicate control.
  • Helpers. Whether the sub's crew appears on the sub's invoices, or whether you pay the helpers directly as separate 1099 vendors. The second pattern is an employee signal for the helpers and often for the lead.
  • Duration and gaps. First and last payment dates, and whether the payment history shows weeks with no activity. Continuous weekly payments for two years with no gaps leave no visible room for other customers. That isn't proof, but it is a flag the DOL's permanence factor cares about.

Then score each sub on the two core factors, using only what the register and the jobsite support. Control points to contractor status when the sub sets the schedule within the milestone, chooses which jobs to take, and can work for others. It points to employee status when your superintendent assigns daily start times, workload, and sequence, or requires exclusivity. Opportunity for profit or loss points to contractor status when the sub can earn more or lose money through pricing, crew decisions, or managing materials and equipment. It points to employee status when the only way to earn more is to work more hours.

Three outcomes come out of that scoring. Green: both core factors point to contractor. Red: both point to employee. Amber: they split, which is exactly when the DOL says the three remaining factors, skill, permanence, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production, decide the question. Green stays as is, with the evidence filed. Red goes to the cost model below and to counsel. Amber goes to counsel first. This scoring is triage from the books, not a legal determination, and it only covers the federal wage and hour tests. The IRS keeps its own common law test of behavioral control, financial control, and relationship, described on its independent contractor page, and the DOL FAQs are explicit that states such as California with an ABC test keep their standards and that you must comply with whichever one provides greater protection.

Here is how it plays at Ridgeline Builders, a fictional general contractor with two open jobs and 23 1099 vendors. Three of them are worth following through the rest of the article.

  • Vendor A is a framing crew lead paid $118,250 in 2026 in weekly invoices of roughly $2,270, billed at $55 an hour. Ridgeline rents the lift, owns the nail guns, and buys the lumber. There is no certificate of insurance on file. The superintendent sets the crew's start time every morning. Both core factors point to employee. Red.
  • Vendor B is a licensed electrical subcontractor paid $212,000 across fixed-price contracts on both jobs, with materials and its own crew on every invoice and a current certificate of insurance. Ridgeline sets milestones, not hours. Both core factors point to contractor. Green.
  • Vendor C is a finish carpenter paid $61,400 at $48 an hour. He brings his own tools and truck and works for two other builders in the gaps that show up in his payment history, but Ridgeline's superintendent schedules his days when he is on site. The core factors split. Amber, to counsel.

Price the cost to convert by job under two wage scenarios

The biggest mistake in conversion math is adding 30 percent to the 1099 rate and calling it the answer. A sub's hourly rate already contains things an employee's wage does not: self-employment tax, their own tools and insurance, unpaid downtime between jobs, and a profit margin. So there are two honest scenarios. Reset the wage to a W-2 equivalent, which the worker may or may not accept. Or carry the 1099 rate as the wage, which is what happens when the conversion is rushed. Price both.

The burden components for 2027 are the employer's 7.65 percent share of Social Security and Medicare, with the 6.2 percent Social Security portion capped at the $184,500 wage base covered in the 2027 wage base article, federal unemployment tax at a net 0.6 percent on the first $7,000, state unemployment tax at your rate notice, workers compensation at the class code rate on your policy, general liability where the premium is rated on payroll, and the overtime premium the FLSA attaches to every hour over 40 in a workweek. Benefits are excluded here. The example uses a 3.0 percent state unemployment rate on a $10,000 wage base, $9.50 per $100 of payroll for workers compensation, and 1.5 percent for general liability. Replace those three with the numbers on your own notices and declarations.

Vendor A worked 2,150 hours in 2026, including about 150 hours in weeks over 40. Here is the annual cost under each scenario.

Annual cost componentKeep as 1099 at $55W-2, wage reset to $44W-2, carry $55 as wage
Base pay (2,150 hours)$118,250$94,600$118,250
Overtime premium (150 hours at half the rate)$0$3,300$4,125
Employer Social Security and Medicare (7.65 percent)$0$7,489$9,362
Federal and state unemployment tax$0$342$342
Workers compensation (assumed $9.50 per $100)$0$9,301$11,626
General liability (assumed 1.5 percent of payroll)$0$1,469$1,836
Total annual cost$118,250$116,501$145,541
Cost per hour$55.00$54.19$67.69

The wage reset lands within 1.5 percent of today's cost. Carrying the rate costs 23 percent more, and workers compensation and overtime are most of the gap. That spread is the negotiation, and it is why the decision belongs to the owner, not to payroll. The worker's side of the math matters too. At $55 on a 1099 he pays both halves of Social Security and Medicare and buys his own tools, so a $44 wage with the employer's half covered is closer to his current take-home than it looks.

Now push it into the jobs. Vendor A has about 1,000 hours left across Ridgeline's two open jobs over the next six months, 600 on Job 101 and 400 on Job 102. Under the carry-the-rate scenario each remaining hour costs $12.69 more, so the estimate to complete rises by $7,614 on Job 101 and $5,076 on Job 102. That changes percent complete, and under the cost-to-cost method it changes earned revenue and the over and under billing lines on the WIP schedule described in the WIP schedule article.

  • Job 101: contract $1,400,000, estimated total cost $1,190,000, cost to date $714,000, billed to date $800,000. Before: 60.0 percent complete, earned revenue $840,000, underbilled $40,000. After: estimated total cost $1,197,614, 59.6 percent complete, earned revenue $834,661, underbilled $34,661. Gross profit at completion falls from $210,000 to $202,386.
  • Job 102: contract $900,000, estimated total cost $765,000, cost to date $306,000, billed to date $380,000. Before: 40.0 percent complete, earned revenue $360,000, overbilled $20,000. After: estimated total cost $770,076, 39.7 percent complete, earned revenue $357,628, overbilled $22,372. Gross profit at completion falls from $135,000 to $129,924.

Under the wage reset scenario the per-hour cost falls by $0.81, so the same jobs move the other way by a few hundred dollars. The point is not the size of the swing on one sub. It is that the conversion decision is a job cost re-estimate, and re-estimates belong in the WIP before the month closes, not in a payroll memo. For a sub whose hours were never tracked by job, the paycheck-to-job tie-out in the service items by paycheck article is the mechanism that makes the W-2 hours land on the right job after conversion.

One more number belongs in the model, and it is not a job cost. If Vendor A was an employee all along under the FLSA, the overtime premium on his past hours was owed. For 150 overtime hours a year at $55, the unpaid premium is $4,125 a year, $8,250 over the two-year lookback, and $12,375 over three years if a court finds the violation willful, each before an equal amount of liquidated damages. Whether to accrue that is an ASC 450 question for the controller and counsel, covered in the controls below.

Accounting controls: source data, calculation, review, and the decision owner

Source data

The register is built from the vendor ledger with 1099-NEC flags, bills and payments by job and account, timesheets or daily logs where they exist, the certificate of insurance file, the workers compensation and general liability declarations, the state unemployment rate notice, and the current estimate to complete by job from the project managers. Nothing in the register is keyed in by hand from a contract. If a field has no source document, it is marked unknown, not assumed.

Deterministic calculation

Given those inputs, the calculation is fixed. Each sub gets a core factor score and a color from evidence rules written down in advance. Each red sub gets the two-scenario cost model using the rates on the notices and declarations. Each open job gets its share of the delta from remaining hours by job, and the WIP recomputes estimated total cost, percent complete, earned revenue, and over or under billing. The misclassification exposure is computed separately from past hours over 40 at the historical rate. Same inputs, same outputs, every month.

Polarity matters when the conversion posts. Today a sub's cost is a flow into job cost: debit cost of revenue, subcontractors, and credit accounts payable. After conversion the same hours post as debit cost of revenue, direct labor, and debit labor burden, with credits to payroll liabilities and accrued burden. Cost to date on the WIP is the cumulative flow. Estimated total cost is a point-in-time estimate that changes the moment the decision is made, not when the first paycheck runs. The exposure reserve, if it meets the ASC 450 threshold of probable and reasonably estimable, is a period expense and a balance sheet liability, debit misclassification expense and credit accrued liabilities, and it does not touch any job.

Reviewer checks

The reviewer ties the register's total 1099 payments to the sum of the subcontractor and related expense accounts and to the 1099-NEC totals filed. The reviewer ties remaining hours by job to the project schedule, confirms the burden rates match the current declarations and rate notice, and confirms that only jobs with a red sub changed in the WIP. The reviewer confirms that no reclassification entry, vendor deactivation, or payroll onboarding happened before the signed decision, and that the 1099-NEC for the year reports only payments made before the cutover date.

Decision owner

The owner or CFO decides each red and amber sub's classification with employment counsel, in writing, with a cutover date. Project managers own the re-estimates that flow from it. The controller owns the exposure reserve and the WIP. Payroll owns onboarding on the cutover date and nothing before it. The register records who decided what and when, because the first question in a DOL audit or a workers compensation premium audit is whether the classification was a considered decision or a habit.

Limits and common mistakes

The rule is narrower than the headlines suggest. It governs the federal wage and hour, family leave, and migrant worker statutes. It does not change the IRS test, the National Labor Relations Act, or state law, and the DOL FAQs say so directly. Several states apply an ABC test, and some apply a construction-specific presumption of employment. A sub who is green under this rule can still be an employee for state unemployment insurance or workers compensation. Run the state test separately for every state you build in. If the IRS answer is also employee, the IRS Voluntary Classification Settlement Program allows prospective reclassification with partial employment tax relief, and that is a tax adviser's call.

The rule is not a safe harbor and it is not retroactive. Written contracts and 1099 forms do not decide status. Practice does. Exposure from past years is governed by the economic reality test the courts applied at the time, and private plaintiffs can still bring claims regardless of which regulation was on the books. The two-year lookback, three if willful, does not reset on January 22.

Common mistakes from the finance side:

  • Pricing conversion as a flat markup on the 1099 rate instead of running the wage reset and the carry scenarios.
  • Converting a sub mid-job without re-estimating the job, so the margin erosion surfaces at completion instead of at the decision.
  • Leaving the vendor record active after conversion and paying the same person through both payables and payroll in the same month.
  • Scoring from the subcontract agreement rather than from the payment history, the invoices, and what the superintendent actually does.
  • Treating the DOL's statement that insurance, safety, and quality requirements don't indicate control as cover for daily scheduling and supplied tools, which do.
  • Forgetting the workers compensation audit. Payments to uninsured subs without a certificate on file are picked up at audit anyway, so a red sub with no certificate is already costing premium.
  • Booking a misclassification reserve as a job cost, or booking none at all because nobody asked the ASC 450 question.

For a contractor on QuickBooks Online, the register above is a vendor-by-job spend report with a handful of added columns, and the WIP effect is a re-estimate per job. FinBoard builds the vendor spend by job and the WIP roll-forward from your QuickBooks data across every entity, so the red subs, the cost deltas, and the over and under billing swing show up in one place before the month closes. You can see how it works at FinBoard.
